title: Clinical validation of a multisensor wearable device (SOUNDI) for the diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)

sections.abstract:
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a common disorder with significant health and economic burdens and the current standard of diagnosis is performed through polysomnography. This study assesed the diagnostic accuracy of SOUNDI, a novel wearable device that uses optical, acoustical, and accelerometer signals for home sleep testing. Fifty patients suspected of having OSA underwent simultaneous monitoring with standard Type 3 cardiorespiratory monitoring (PG) and SOUNDI system. The apnea‒hypopnea index (AHI), oxygen desaturation index and oxygen saturation parameters derived from SOUNDI were highly correlated (r = 0.87–0.99, p < 0.0001) and were in good agreement with the PG. SOUNDI study was shown to have excellent specificity and positive predictive value (PPV) at various AHI values ( AHI 5/h: specificity = 0.769, PPV = 0.919; AHI 15/h: specificity = 0.852, PPV = 0.833; AHI 30/h: specificity = 0.833, PPV = 0.100). Patient feedback highlighted significant satisfaction with the wearingability and ease of use of the SOUNDI, indicating a preference for multi-night monitoring. The findings suggest that the SOUNDI offers a patient-centric and potentially cost-effective alternative to PG for OSA diagnosis in the home setting.

Subject terms: Diseases, Engineering, Health care, Medical research
sections.introduction:
Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is the most common sleep-related breathing disorder. It is characterized by partial or complete upper airway obstructions that are associated with intermittent hypoxia and transient arousals. OSA, which is associated with excessive daytime sleepiness and increased cardiovascular risk, significantly increases mortality and morbidity in the affected population, constituting a public health problem. The global prevalence of OSA in middle-aged adults has been estimated to be nearly one billion, with approximately half of these individuals having moderate-to-severe disease with an indication for treatment 1 .

The current standard of diagnosis is performed through polysomnography (PSG) examinations, which can be conducted either at the patient’s home or in a hospital setting. PSG relies on the nocturnal collection of various vital parameters to provide an objective quantification of the number, characteristics, and intensity of apneas and hypopneas.

Alternative ambulatory methods have been developed for more efficient use of healthcare resources. For diagnosis of OSA, several devices are currently available to be worn at home by patients during sleep. Sleep monitoring devices are classified according to completeness of the signals recorded and presence of a technician overnight 2 . Type 1 monitoring is the complete PSG recording in the sleep laboratory monitored by a technician, while type 2–4 monitoring devices provide unattended recordings from full PSG (type 2), to four- to eight-channel (type 3) or one to three-channel (type 4) recordings.

Type 3 cardiorespiratory monitoring (PG) during sleep is increasingly used in the diagnosis of OSA. Underdiagnosis of OSA in the general population and the rising prevalence of obesity worldwide have increased the number of patients referred to sleep centres for suspected sleep apnoea. In addition, the continuing search for cost-effective diagnostic and therapeutic approaches makes type 3 portable devices very attractive to deal with a very large number of suspected OSA patients 3 .

The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) guidelines strongly recommend the use of Home Sleep Apnea Testing (HSAT) over no testing for suspected OSA, provided the device meets Type 3 or Type 4 monitoring standards 4 .

We proposed an innovative, non-invasive wearable alternative to conventional PG, the SOUNDI device (Biocubica S.r.l., Milan, Italy). SOUNDI is engineered to acquire various multimodal surrogate physiological signals that reflect cardiorespiratory function during sleep. A key feature of the system is its integration of advanced sensors and signal processing algorithms, which allows to estimate key cardiorespiratory and sleep metrics with minimal patient compliance burden. Figure 1 provides an overview of the SOUNDI device and its application for sleep monitoring.

( a ) The SOUNDI recording unit. The reverse side illustrates the custom-designed bell-shape, the optical sensor and a connection port (e.g., USB-C) for data or charging. ( b ) Illustrates a typical data output view from the SOUNDI system software. The trace displays multiple physiological signals simultaneously (e.g., cardiorespiratory, movement, acoustic data) with automatic event scoring (e.g., “Apnea” and “Hypoapnea” events marked in red). The time scale is visible along the top, and various channels, along with summary metrics (such as the Desaturation Index), are presented at the bottom. ( c ) Patient Setup Diagram: Shows the typical application of the wearable device to the patient for nocturnal monitoring. The diagram highlights the placement of the SOUNDI core unit and associated ECG 1-lead on the body, and traditional PG system with Respiratory Inductance Plethysmography (RIP) belts placed around the thorax (chest) and abdomen for respiratory effort, the nasal cannula for nasal pressure/flow, a pulse oximeter sensor attached to a finger for SaO 2 and heart rate.

This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of the SOUNDI system in patients with suspected OSA in comparison against PG.
sections.methods:
The trial, which was a single-center, prospective study, was designed in adherence to the ISO Standard on Clinical Investigation of Medical Devices for Human Subjects EN ISO 14,155:20,120 [ https://www.iso.org/standard/71690.html ]. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations. The study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee of Istituto Auxologico Italiano IRCCS and was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki (1964) and its later amendments. Informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their enrolment in the study. The clinical trial was prospectively registered on ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT06320795 ) on 22 November 2023.

The study was carried out in the Sleep Center Unit of San Luca Hospital (Istituto Auxologico Italiano, Milan, Italy).

The primary endpoint was to evaluate the accuracy of the clinical diagnosis of OSA assisted by the home sleep study with SOUNDI against the clinical diagnosis assisted by PG as the reference standard. The secondary endpoint of the trial was to evaluate the agreement between the AHI from the home sleep study with SOUNDI and the home sleep study with PG in patients referred to sleep clinics with suggestive OSA symptoms.

Patients were given details in advance about the study, both verbally and in writing. On the day of their sleep study, patients were first set up with the complete suite of conventional PG sensors. The SOUNDI sensor was subsequently applied.

Adjustments were made to the PG by the technician if there was a lead-off or poor signal quality (as per the standard of care). It was not possible for the technicians to monitor the SOUNDI signals, so adjustments were not made to this system.

The trial included consecutive adult patients aged 18–70 years who were referred to the sleep center for possible sleep apnea diagnosis. The exclusion criteria included having a known allergy to any material of the device, having electronic body implants and being pregnant.

Home sleep apnea testing with nocturnal polygraphy was completed in all patients, with the device routinely used (Embletta MPR PG -Natus Medical, California) recording nasal airflow (nasal cannula), thoracic and abdominal movement sensors (respiratory inductance plethysmography), one-channel electrocardiogram (ECG), body position, oxygen saturation, and snoring.

The polygraphic recorder was positioned in the early evening, and the correct position of the nasal cannula before bedtime was explained to the patient. After the conclusion of the home night recording, the polygraph was returned to the outpatient facility the following day.

The device under evaluation in this study, SOUNDI, is a wearable multisensor device measuring 6.0 cm in diameter and 1.2 cm in height and weighing 35 g (Fig. 1 a). The device attaches to the thorax, between the second and third intercostal space, with a disposable medical-grade adhesive.

The device, which was previously described 9 – 12 , is based on a patented technology (Patent N.EP3248541A1) and consists of a multiple-sensor device featuring simultaneous recording of optical, acoustic, accelerometer and 1-lead electrical, body and ambient temperature signals. A digital optical sensor records the PPG signal. The acoustic signal is recorded via a digital differential air-pressure sensor coupled with a custom-designed bell-shaped chassis (details about principles, design, and implementation can be found in 9–12). One digital six-axis inertial measurement unit (IMU) provides the acceleration and angular speed encoded in a quaternion, which is useful for posture, motion detection and thorax and abdomen movements and might also be used for noise mitigation. The IMU measures the device’s orientation relative to the gravitational vector. An algorithm classifies the body’s orientation based on the roll (rotation around the anterior–posterior axis) and pitch (rotation around the lateral axis) angles. The supine position is classified when the orientation falls within a predefined angular tolerance (e.g., ± 5 or ± 5 10 degrees) of the perfectly supine orientation (patient lying on their back). Three electric terminals are devoted to plugging wired electrodes placed on the thorax to acquire a single derivation ECG analog signal (1-lead ECG recorder), which is digitized directly on board and is usable primarily for basic heart monitoring and bioimpedance. One digital temperature sensor is placed on the contact surface to record the body temperature. The Bosch BME680 sensor provides ambient temperature, humidity, and volatile organic compound monitoring for air quality evaluation. The main functionalities (e.g., start and stop time, acquisition protocol and duration, battery status, enabling/disabling sensors, and signal quality verification) are controllable via a software PC, SOUNDI DOC. The software SOUNDI DOC allows the clinician to set up the sleep study for individual patients and visualize/review its outcomes (Fig. 1 b).

Following the completion of a sleep study, if both the SOUNDI and traditional PG sleep studies met the study acceptance criteria (see below), the recordings were anonymized, randomized and sent to four independent sleep professionals, who used RemLogic software (version 1.3, Embla Systems Ltd., Kanata, Canada) to score the studies according to the AASM guidelines 13 . The sleep professionals were blinded to the patient ID and sleep study device used for each recording.

The data were inspected to assess signal quality and completeness. A successful study was defined as a study in which:

The SOUNDI study and the traditional PG study had ≥ 6 hours of time in bed and

The recording of ≥4 hours of the study consisted of sleep and

All signals essential for scoring according to the AASM criteria were present.

The essential signals for the sleep study following the AASM guidelines were the SaO 2 signal, breathing efforts (thorax and/or abdomen signal), and airflow (nasal pressure).

The following parameters were calculated:

Apnea hypopnea index (AHI) total and supine

AHI obstructive

Oxygen desaturation index (ODI)

Average arterial oxygen saturation (SaO 2 )

Minimum SaO 2

Percentage of sleep time with SaO 2 < 90%

Average heart rate

Minimum heart rate

Percentage of sleep time in the supine position

At the end of the study, the diagnostic results derived from the PG were compared with those from the SOUNDI.

Respiratory events were scored as apnea when there was a drop ≥ 90% of the airflow lasting at least 10 s. Events were scored as hypopnea if a decrease ≥ 30% of the airflow occurred for at least 10 s with a fall in SaO 2 ≥ 3% compared with the preceding baseline level.

The AHI was calculated as the total number of apneas and hypopneas per hour of sleep. Moderate-severe OSA was defined as an AHI ≥ 15–30 events per hour, mild OSA was defined as an AHI ≥ 5, and no OSA was defined as an AHI < 5 events per hour. The ODI was defined as the number of falls in SaO 2 ≥ 3% per hour of sleep.

Patient feedback regarding the usability, comfort, and confidence of using the SOUNDI device was collected via a questionnaire.

A descriptive analysis of the study parameters was performed. The data are presented as the means ± standard deviations (SDs). Pearson’s correlation coefficients and Bland‒Altman plots were used to assess the correlation and agreement between the polysomnographic data and the SOUNDI data. The concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) was calculated for all sleep variables to estimate the agreement and precision in performance between the two devices.

We analyzed the sensitivity and specificity, and the positive and negative predictive values of the home monitoring, in relation to AHI, considering the PG to be the standard (gold standard).

All the statistical analyses were conducted via SigmaPlot software and Python. A p value < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

The sample size for this study was determined based on a formal power calculation, aimed at assessing the agreement between the parameters detected by the investigational SOUNDI method and those measured by PG. A sample of 50 evaluable patients is required to ensure a statistical power of 90% (1-β = 0.90) in determining if the parameter values detected by the SOUNDI method agree with those measured by PG. The sample size was calculated using PASS 2021 (Power Analysis and Sample Size Software (2021). NCSS, LLC. Kaysville, Utah, USA).
sections.results:
Consecutive patients referred for clinical suspicion of OSA to San Luca Hospital, Istituto Auxologico Italiano IRCCS in Milan, between October 2023 and October 2024 were enrolled in this study. They underwent simultaneous cardiorespiratory nocturnal monitoring (PG) and a SOUNDI device.

A total of 50 participants were included, 36 (72%) of whom were males. The mean (SD) age was 52.3 (12.5) years. Table 1 shows the demographic characteristics of the patients.

Demographic characteristic data of the study group.

All recruited subjects completed the investigation and were included in the final analysis. No subjects were excluded due to device failure or refusal to continue.

All polygraphic examinations and soundi-derived signals were automatically scored by dedicated software and then manually scored by a sleep-certified specialist who was unaware of the patients’ identities.

Table 2 shows the PG and SOUNDI results of all sleep variables and the CCC analysis results.

PG and SOUNDI results and CCC of all sleep parameters.

Overall, we see high correlation in all sleep variables (. > 68). The highest CCC was found to be in AHI (0.98), ODI (0.97), and SaO 2 mean (0.94), indicating that SOUNDI performs well in comparison to the traditional PG system in detection of OSA.

Bland–Altman analysis and correlation coefficients (Pearson) to compare SOUNDI’s absolute measurements with those of the PG/reference monitor are reported in Figs. 2 and 3 .

Scatter plots comparing PG and SOUNDI device values.

Bland‒Altman diagrams comparing PG and SOUNDI device values.

A strong correlation (r = 0.99, p < 0.0001) and good agreement were found between AHI PG and AHI S (Figs. 2 a and 3 a). Similarly, there was a strong correlation (r = 0.93 and r = 0.97 with p < 0.0001) and good agreement between the AHI-sup PG and the AHI-sup S (Fig. 2 b and 3 b) and between the AHI-obs PG and the AHI-obs S (r = 0.97, p < 0.0001). The ODI measured from PG was 18.7 (21.2), whereas that from SOUNDI was 17.4 (18.0), with a high correlation (r = 0.98, p < 0.0001) and good agreement (Figs. 2 c and 3 c).

A high correlation (r = 0.93, p < 0.0001) and good agreement were also found between the SaO 2 mean PG and SaO 2 mean (Figs. 2 d and 3 d) and between SaO 2 min PG and SaO 2 min S (Figs. 2 e and 3 e). Similarly, there was also a high correlation (r = 0.91, p < 0.0001) and good agreement between PG SaO 2 < 90% and SOUNDI SaO 2 < 90%.

The mean bpm from PG was 61.6 (7.4), whereas that from SOUNDI was 64.3 (6.9), with a good correlation (r = 0.87, p < 0,0001), and the mean bpm from PG was 47.8 (6.1), whereas that from SOUNDI was 48.4 (7.4), with a good correlation (r = 0.73, p < 0,0001) (Figs. 2 f–g and 3 f–g).

A good correlation (r = 0.80, p < 0,0001) and good agreement were also found between sleep time in the supine position measured via the PG and the SOUNDI (Figs. 2 h and 3 h).

On the basis of the standard cutoffs of the AHI 5, 15, 30 events/h, 34%, 14% and 22% of participants had mild, moderate, and severe OSA according to the PG, respectively, whereas the percentages of participants with SOUNDI scores were 34%, 16% and 20%, respectively.

Table 3 shows the sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value and area under curve of the SOUNDI, when compared against simultaneous PG. SOUNDI study was shown to have excellent specificity and positive predictive value at various AHI values.

Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, positive likelihood ratio, negative likelihood ratio and AUC of the SOUNDI device, when compared with simultaneous PG.

AUC, area under curve, LR + , positive likelihood ratio; LR-, negative likelihood ratio; NPV, negative predictive value; PPV, positive predictive value.

The ROC curves are shown in Fig. 4 . The results between the PG study and the SOUNDI were almost identical in all values.

Receiver–operator characteristic curves (ROC) of the PG AHI and SOUNDI AHI.

To assess the inter-rater agreement between the SOUNDI device and the PG reference system in classifying the severity of OSA, Cohen’s Kappa coefficient was calculated. For this analysis, OSA severity was categorized into four levels based on AHI: 0 (Absent: AHI < 5), 1 (Mild: AHI ≥ 5), 2 (Moderate: AHI ≥ 15), and 3 (Severe: AHI ≥ 30). Table 4 shows the confusion matrix for OSA severity classification. This result demonstrates a robust level of agreement, highlighting the clinical utility of the SOUNDI device in providing consistent severity classifications when compared to the established PG.

Confusion matrix for OSA severity classification (SOUNDI vs. PG).

Figure 5 presents the distributions of the AHI and ODI values for both the output of the SOUNDI and the PG for different severity categories and for increasing BMI, showing that the anthropometric characteristics of the patients do not affect the correlation between the two devices (PG and SOUNDI). Additionally, as shown in Fig. 6 , both devices showed that men had significantly greater AHI and ODI values than females did. These differences in nocturnal home sleep cardiorespiratory monitoring could reflect different pathophysiological mechanisms of OSAS onset between the two sexes, which should be investigated in future scientific studies 5 , 6 .

( a ) Distributions of the AHI and ODI values of both the SOUNDI and the reference PG for different severity categories and ( b ) increasing BMI.

Influence of sex on the AHI and ODI for both the SOUNDI and the reference PG.

The patients were asked to complete a questionnaire with four questions regarding satisfaction (‘how satisfied are you with the wearability of the SOUNDI device compared with the standard PG?’), the positioning procedure (‘how satisfied are you with the ease of positioning the SOUNDI device compared with the standard PG’), and the willingness to use the SOUNDI device (‘Would you wear the SOUNDI device for multiple nights for continuous monitoring’). In addition, the patients were given the option of writing down comments about the experience. Overall, the comments revealed how patients were impressed with the device, the ease of use and very much preferred it to the standard PG.

In terms of satisfaction, 78% of the patients reported that the score was completely satisfactory (score: 5), 16% rated it as 4, and 4% rated it as 3. Only 1 patient gave a score of 2, with no patients expressing complete dissatisfaction. Eighty-six percent reported that the positioning procedure was easy (score: 5), whereas 12% rated the ease of installation as 4 and 2% as 3. No patients rated the ease of installation as 1 or 2. Similarly, 84% of the respondents reported their willingness to use the device in the future for multiple nights for continuous monitoring, whereas 16% reported their willingness to use it for multiple night recordings.
sections.discussion:
The evolution of wearable devices has transformed sleep monitoring through advancements in sensor technology and ergonomics 7 . This study demonstrated that SOUNDI, a novel multisensor device (optical, acoustic via a differential air pressure sensor, and accelerometer signals), accurately quantifies obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) during home sleep testing, with a diagnostic accuracy comparable to that of cardiorespiratory polygraphy (PG).

SOUNDI processes signals to derive data on breathing, chest-wall effort, oxygenation, posture, and snoring. Despite deriving diagnostic parameters from indirect physiological signals, the accuracy of the SOUNDI aligns with that of the PG, as evidenced by the high correlations and good agreement found for key parameters such as the AHI, ODI, and SaO 2 .

Data collected from both the PG and the SOUNDI indicate that patients’ anthropometric characteristics do not affect the correlation between the two devices. Furthermore, both devices revealed that men had significantly greater AHI and ODI values than women did.

The demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy and strong agreement metrics achieved by the SOUNDI device validate its performance against the standard PG. Crucially, the system’s inherent portability, minimal setup requirements, and validated reliability position it as a highly feasible and cost-effective alternative for screening and definitive diagnosis in non-specialized clinical settings, effectively mitigating the logistical and resource constraints inherent to in-laboratory monitoring.

Patient experience is increasingly recognized as a key metric in healthcare 8 . Patient feedback revealed a clear preference for the SOUNDI over the PG, with 86% of patients finding the positioning procedure completely easy and 78% being completely satisfied with the wearability. Eighty-four percent of the respondents expressed a willingness to use SOUNDI for future multi-night monitoring. These results confirm that the SOUNDI meets patient expectations regarding ease of use and comfort, which are essential factors for widespread adoption.

Operational differences exist between the two devices.

In the traditional PG system, respiratory flow is directly recorded by a nasal cannula measuring changes in nasal air pressure during ventilation, which are used to detect and classify sleep events. In the SOUNDI device, respiratory flow is derived from an integrated analysis of respiratory movements (thorax and abdomen).

SOUNDI is a patch-based device with sensors integrated so that its position is reliable and consistent throughout the recording period. In contrast, the respiratory bands in the traditional PG system face the possibility of band dislodgment.

The statistically small difference was found in concurrently recorded SaO 2 values, which were slightly greater when obtained at the chest by the SOUNDI than when obtained from the finger by the PG. We believe that this difference may be due to either changes in the peripheral vasculature of the patients or technical differences between the SaO 2 sensors, such as the sampling rate and artifact removal algorithms.

Despite these strengths, our study has several limitations. First, our study recruited patients consecutively via a real-life approach without any selection based on comorbidities. Future research should investigate the performance of the SOUNDI in specific populations, such as those with metabolic disorders such as diabetes, respiratory diseases such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or cardiovascular diseases such as chronic congestive heart failure.

Second, the SOUNDI system does not include real-time attended supervision during setting and positioning. The accurate positioning of devices is a critical aspect for outcomes that rely on sensor contact. In summary, care should be taken to ensure optimal fit and sensor positioning, and clear instructions should be provided to the study participants regarding wearing time and, potentially, manual adjustments of the collected data. The same sensors, positioning, and adjustments should be used consistently for the entire duration of the study. The development of real-time attended supervision functionalities is planned for future versions of the system. It should be acknowledged as a limitation that the gold-standard in-laboratory Polysomnography (PSG) was not available as the reference standard for the definitive diagnosis of Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) in this specific setting.
sections.conclusion: In conclusion, SOUNDI demonstrates significant advancements in home sleep testing, offering comparable diagnostic accuracy to standard polygraphy with enhanced patient experience and potential for cost-effective, accessible healthcare solutions. Moreover, future studies should focus on validating its performance in specific patient populations and exploring its potential for long-term monitoring and therapeutic intervention.
